turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): I'll get these on the chart before Dr Meehan sees you. Blood pressure 138 over 84, pulse 88, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air, temperature 36.8, and respirations 20.
[SEG0002] person_1 (NURSE): Spirometry, best of three blows: FEV1 1.62 litres, 54 percent predicted, FVC 3.1 litres, ratio 52 percent. He's a bit puffed after it.
[SEG0003] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, that's grand. Come on in and sit down. I'm Dr Meehan. What's been the main bother?
[SEG0004] person_3 (PATIENT): Doctor, I'm worried sick. I've a cough every morning and I can't get a breath, and I keep thinking it's something terrible.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll go through it properly, no rushing. Tell me about that cough, how long it's been with you.
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): Years, if I'm honest. But the last three weeks, since the chest infection, I'm hacking every morning. My uncle had lung cancer. Is three weeks long enough for that?
[SEG0007] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'm Sinead, his carer, I come weekday mornings. The cough starts before he's up, and it's been rougher since that infection, I'd say.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): A morning cough has a few causes, and we'll not leap to the worst one. Is there phlegm, or any blood in it?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Yellowy stuff in the mornings. No blood, not a drop. The infection itself was about a month ago.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you get an antibiotic for it?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Um, from the chemist, amoxicillin, 500 milligrams three times a day for a week. I finished the box ten days ago, or was it two weeks. I can't pin the date at all.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's fine, the exact day won't change the plan. Any fever on you now, or night sweats?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): No fever. I was boiling with the infection but that's gone. No sweats either.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the breathlessness, when do you notice it?

[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): On the way to the shop, or the stairs. I have to stop halfway up. It's been worse this past fortnight. The nurse said 94 percent, is that dangerous? Will I be put on oxygen?
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): 94 sitting here is lower than I'd like, but it's not an emergency and I'm not reaching for oxygen today. Do you get a wheeze, a whistle in the chest?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No wheeze. I don't have that.
[SEG0018] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He does be wrecked after the stairs. I do the hoovering now, he can't manage the landing.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any pain in the chest, or swelling around the ankles?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): No chest pain. Ankles are grand, no swelling. Should I be watching the ankles? Is it the heart?
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Worth asking, and no swelling is a good sign. We'll listen in a minute. What inhalers are you on?

[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): The blue inhaler when I'm gasping, two puffs. And the purple inhaler, I'm supposed to take two puffs morning and night, only I forget. Is the purple one a steroid? I read they melt your bones.

[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): The blue one is salbutamol, your reliever. The purple one is Seretide, a steroid with a long-acting partner, and at these doses the bone risk is small. How many days do you actually take the purple one?
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): Maybe once a day. Some days I don't touch it. If I start taking it right, will the cough stop?
[SEG0025] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He misses it more often than not. The purple inhaler is still in the carton half the mornings I come in.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the smoking. How many in a day, roughly?
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): About ten a day. Well, actually, maybe twenty, depends on the day. I've smoked since I was sixteen and I'm sixty-two now. If I quit, is it too late entirely?
[SEG0028] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Nearer the twenty, doctor. I've seen him open a second packet.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not too late at all. The cough and the breathing can ease off if you stop. Did you ever try to quit?
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): I tried the patches once. They made me queasy so I stopped after a few days. Is there something else, or am I stuck with them?
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): There's more than patches. Any other tablets, blood pressure or the like?
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): A water tablet for the blood pressure, one every morning. I think it's 2.5 of something. Does that affect the lungs? Should I stop it?
[SEG0033] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Don't stop it, the GP started it. The name's on the box at home, little white tablets, I just can't call the name to mind. He never misses that one.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Keep taking it, don't stop it on my account. Bring the box next time. Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): No, nothing. No allergies. Are you going to give me more tablets? I get anxious with new ones.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Sorry, I have to go back on the wheeze. At night I do get a whistle, especially lying flat, and it wakes me. I told you I didn't, but I do.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm glad you said it. So it wakes you, worse when you lie flat. How are you fixed for pillows?
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): Two, sometimes three if it's bad. Is that heart failure? Please don't soften it.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): A whistle lying flat is very often the airways themselves. Heart failure is less likely with no ankle swelling, but I'm not brushing your worry off. Let me listen.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chest looks a little hyperinflated. There's scattered wheeze both sides, no crackles. Heart sounds are normal, and I can't see any ankle swelling.
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): Scattered wheeze, God. She said the ratio was 52 percent. Does that mean my lungs are half gone? Am I going to die of this?

[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): It means the air leaves slowly, an obstructive pattern, not that half the lung is missing. Putting the smoking, the morning cough, the wheeze and those numbers together, my working impression is COPD, and there may still be some hangover from the chest infection. I wouldn't call either one definite today.
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): COPD. Right. That's not cancer, is it? You'd tell me if it was cancer?
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): COPD is not cancer. Nothing today screams cancer, but I'd still like a chest x-ray so we're not guessing.
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): When can I have that? And do I keep the two inhalers, or will you change them?

[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll book the x-ray from reception, hopefully this week. Stay on both: purple inhaler two puffs morning and night, every single day, and the blue one two puffs when you're gasping. No new inhaler from me today.
[SEG0047] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll leave the purple one beside the kettle. He never misses the tea.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lovely. I'd like to refer you to the HSE stop-smoking service as well. They can try gum or a tablet if the patches turned your stomach, and there's no charge.
[SEG0049] person_3 (PATIENT): What if I can't stick it? I get ratty without a cigarette. And if the x-ray is clear, am I grand then?

[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ratty is normal, they'll expect it. A clear film would ease the cancer worry, it wouldn't cancel the COPD picture. Come back and see me in six weeks with the result. If you're gasping at rest, or you cough up blood, don't wait the six weeks, come straight back or go to the emergency department.
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): Six weeks, okay. I also get a bit of heartburn after the tea. Is that making the cough worse? Sorry, I know I'm asking a pile of questions.

[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ask away. Heartburn can irritate a cough in some people, but it doesn't fit as the main cause here. Mention it again if it's bothering you and we'll look at it next time. Anything else on your mind?
[SEG0053] person_3 (PATIENT): No, that's me done. Thanks for explaining it, I was up the walls coming in.
[SEG0054] person_4 (CAREGIVER): We'll bring the tablet box, and I'll get him to the x-ray. Come on, you.
